package_info.package_manager: N/A (malware binary, not a package manager ecosystem)
package_info.why_malicious: The CrySIS/Dharma ransomware family is designed to encrypt user files, delete system recovery data, persist across reboots, and extort victims for payment. Its behavior is intentionally destructive and criminal, with no legitimate use case.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: SetConsoleCP(1251); // Set codepage to support Cyrillic languages
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code sets the console codepage to 1251, enabling display of Cyrillic characters, which facilitates communication with Russian-speaking victims.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Changing the codepage to a Cyrillic locale is uncommon for legitimate software unless specifically targeting Russian-speaking users. In ransomware, this is used to display ransom notes in the attacker's language.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal software does not alter the system codepage unless required for localization; ransomware does this to ensure ransom instructions are readable.
key_indicators: Preparation for non-English ransom note display

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code invokes vssadmin.exe to delete all shadow copies, preventing system recovery and backup restoration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Deleting shadow copies is a well-known anti-recovery tactic used by ransomware to prevent victims from restoring files without paying the ransom.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not delete system backups or shadow copies without explicit user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Backup management tools may delete old shadow copies as part of maintenance.
key_indicators: Silent deletion of all shadow copies

required_permissions: write access to user startup folders

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code copies itself to the user's Startup folder to ensure persistence across reboots.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Self-replication to the Startup folder is a classic persistence mechanism for malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installers may add shortcuts, but not copy entire executables for persistence without user approval.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate applications add auto-start entries, but not by copying the main binary.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: For each file in user directories: Encrypt file and append custom extension
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code iterates over user files, encrypts them, and appends a custom extension identifying the ransomware variant.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Mass file encryption with custom extensions is the core behavior of ransomware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not encrypt user files en masse without user intent.

required_permissions: write access to multiple system/user directories

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Write Info.hta to: C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup, C:\Users\<victim>\AppData\Roaming, C:\Users\<victim>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup, C:\Windows\System32
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After encryption, the code writes a ransom note (Info.hta) to multiple locations to ensure the victim sees payment instructions.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Dropping ransom notes in multiple locations is a hallmark of ransomware, maximizing the chance the victim will see the instructions.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not create ransom notes or demand payment.
key_indicators: Use of .hta file for ransom instructions

required_permissions: write access to root and desktop directories

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Write info.txt to: C:\, C:\Users\Public\Desktop, C:\Users\<victim>\Desktop
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After encryption, the code writes a text file with contact instructions to the root and desktop directories.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Dropping contact instructions in prominent locations is a common ransomware tactic.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not demand ransom or provide criminal contact information.
key_indicators: Files placed in root and desktop directories

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After encryption, the code launches mshta.exe to display the ransom note to the victim.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Launching mshta.exe to display a ransom note is a direct method to ensure the victim sees payment instructions.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not use mshta.exe to display extortion messages.

attack_chain.action: Initial execution of ransomware binary, sets codepage for ransom note display.
Deletes shadow copies to prevent file recovery.
Copies itself to Startup folder for persistence.
Encrypts user files and appends custom extension.
Drops ransom notes (Info.hta, info.txt) in multiple locations.
Launches mshta.exe to display ransom note to victim.

behavioral_signatures: Execution of vssadmin.exe to delete all shadow copies
Self-copying to Startup folders for persistence
Bulk file encryption with custom extensions
Dropping and launching Info.hta via mshta.exe
Creation of ransom notes in multiple user/system directories
file_indicators: Info.hta in Startup, System32, and user AppData folders
info.txt in root and desktop directories
Presence of ransomware binary in Startup folder
network_indicators: Typically, CrySIS/Dharma does not exfiltrate data but may include attacker contact details in ransom notes; network indicators may include connections to attacker email or chat services as specified in ransom notes
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for execution of vssadmin.exe with arguments to delete shadow copies, creation of Info.hta and info.txt in system/user directories, mass file renaming with new extensions, and execution of mshta.exe with Info.hta as an argument. Alert on binaries self-replicating to Startup folders and on the sudden appearance of ransom notes or bulk file encryption activity.
